278	### Enqueueing: `enqueue` vs `enqueue_keyed`
279	
280	From inside any transaction — a route handler, a job handler, a cron tick
281	— `tx.enqueue(job)` writes the job into that same committing log record;
282	`Db::transact`'s apply step materializes it as a row in the platform's
283	`charpente.jobs` table. `tx.enqueue_keyed(key, job)` does the same, plus
284	carries a key: the app's own identity for the job. It is not the idempotency
285	key an outbound call sends: the platform mints that one itself, for every
286	outbound job, keyed or not ("Outbound jobs" below). On a bare `Tx` these take
287	`global` jobs. A `scoped_by` job is enqueued the same two ways on its tenant's
288	`ScopedTx` (above). Inside the deterministic boundary
289	the key means nothing in v0 — it is carried, never indexed or deduped on,
290	because exactly-once state effects here are structural (below), not
291	key-based. An empty key is a contract panic: ``"contract: an `enqueue_keyed`
292	app key names the job's external identity — it cannot be empty"``.
293	
294	```rust
295	use charpente::core::table::Id;
296	use charpente::http::ApiError;
297	use charpente::kernel::JobError;
298	use charpente::{Tx, View, job, route, table};
299	
300	#[table(global)]
301	struct Invoice {
302	    id: Id<Invoice>,
303	    finalized: bool,
304	}
305	
306	#[job(global)]
307	struct SendReminder {
308	    invoice: u64,
309	}
310	
311	impl SendReminder {
312	    fn run(self, _tx: &mut Tx) -> Result<(), JobError> {
313	        Ok(())
314	    }
315	}
316	
317	#[route(POST "/invoices/:id/remind", public)]
318	fn remind(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Invoice>) -> Result<(), ApiError> {
319	    let mut inv = tx.get(id)?.ok_or(ApiError::NotFound)?;
320	    inv.finalized = true;
321	    tx.put(&inv);
322	    // `SendReminder.invoice` stays a bare `u64`: a job payload is never
323	    // itself a wire type (it never crosses HTTP), so it has no `Wire`
324	    // requirement — only `#[route]` params/bodies/responses/errors do.
325	    tx.enqueue_keyed(
326	        format!("reminder:{}", id.raw()),
327	        SendReminder { invoice: id.raw() },
328	    );
329	    Ok(())
330	}
331	```
332	
333	### Retry, dead-letter, and exactly-once effects
334	
335	The dispatcher runs the earliest-due job inline, on the kernel thread, as
336	its own transaction. On `Ok`, the handler's own effects (puts, deletes,
337	enqueues, emits) and the row's Done-mark commit **as one record** — there
338	is no window where the effects are durable but the Done-mark isn't, or
339	vice versa: exactly-once state effects, structurally.
340	
341	On `Err(JobError::App(msg))` — your handler's own rejection, a panic inside
342	it (absorbed as `"handler panicked: <payload>"`), or a payload that does not
343	decode under its own recorded shape (`"job decode for <Name>: <e> — its
344	recorded shape is this binary's, so either …"`: corrupt bytes, or a change
345	inside a type one of its fields holds, §12; a Pending job of another shape is
346	refused before dispatch can start, and this binary refuses to enqueue one —
347	see "Changing a job's fields") — that attempt's own effects never committed, and a *second*
348	transaction records the failure: `attempts` increments, `last_error` gets
349	the message, and:
350	
351	- if `attempts < retry.max`: stays Pending, `due_at` (a `WallTime`, so a
352	  restart keeps the wait) moves to the wall-clock `now + backoff *
353	  2^(attempts - 1)` (nanoseconds; doubles every attempt, saturating rather
354	  than overflowing at absurd attempt counts) — the policy's configured base
355	  `backoff` is attempt 1's wait.
356	- if `attempts >= retry.max`: status becomes Dead. Dead rows are retained,
357	  with `last_error` as the record of what killed them.
358	
359	On `Err(JobError::Io(e))` — a platform fault the handler's own reads
360	surfaced, or one from the transaction machinery itself — none of this
361	happens: it is **not an attempt**, a `TableReadRefusal` excepted: it is
362	the handler's own deterministic bug, an attempt (§4). Otherwise the row
363	stays Pending, untouched, and
364	the error bubbles up (restart-and-recover, same as a request-path `Io`
365	failure in §5) instead of silently burning retry budget on a healthy job
366	that just hit a bad disk. `JobError::Io`'s own `Display` names this:
367	`"platform IO failure during the handler (not an attempt): <e>"`.
368	
369	One more failure mode: if a `JobRow`'s `name` isn't in the `jobs![...]` list
370	`App::mount_jobs` was given — a job enqueued by a since-removed or renamed
371	type — it fails the same way as a handler rejection, with: `"job
372	\"<name>\" is not registered — add it to the jobs![…] list passed to
373	App::mount_jobs (or this log outlived a renamed job type)"`.
374	
375	### Outbound jobs: calling the world after commit
376	
377	A job that calls an outside service over HTTP declares the host it calls with
378	`outbound = "<host>"`, and writes two methods in place of `run`. `call` reads what
379	it needs and builds the request. The kernel sends it outside any transaction, since
380	no transaction waits on the network, and hands the reply to `settle`, which commits
381	the reply's consequences in the transaction that marks the job Done.
382	Enqueue one the way you enqueue any job, from a route, a job or a cron tick:
383	`enqueue`, `enqueue_keyed`, `enqueue_in` and cron take outbound jobs unchanged.
384	
385	```rust
386	use charpente::kernel::JobError;
387	use charpente::outbound::{Call, IdempotencyKey, Reply};
388	use charpente::{Tx, job};
389	
390	#[job(
391	    global,
392	    outbound = "pay.test",
393	    retry(max = 3, backoff = "1s"),
394	    timeout = "2s"
395	)]
396	struct Charge {
397	    cents: u64,
398	}
399	
400	impl Charge {
401	    fn call(&self, _tx: &Tx, key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError> {
402	        Ok(Some(
403	            Call::post("/charges")
404	                .header("idempotency-key", key.as_str())
405	                .form(&[("amount", self.cents.to_string())]),
406	        ))
407	    }
408	
409	    fn settle(self, _tx: &mut Tx, reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError> {
410	        match reply.status() {
411	            200 => Ok(()),
412	            s => Err(JobError::app(format!("pay.test answered {s}"))),
413	        }
414	    }
415	}
416	
417	#[job(global, outbound = "mail.test")]
418	struct Mail {}
419	
420	impl Mail {
421	    fn call(&self, _tx: &Tx, _key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError> {
422	        Ok(None)
423	    }
424	
425	    fn settle(self, _tx: &mut Tx, _reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError> {
426	        Ok(())
427	    }
428	}
429	
430	// One `Host` per host a mounted job calls, in any order.
431	use charpente::core::db::Schema;
432	use charpente::core::io::{Disk, Entropy};
433	use charpente::http::{App, AppConfig};
434	use charpente::jobs;
435	use charpente::outbound::Host;
436	
437	fn build_app(disk: Box<dyn Disk>, entropy: Box<dyn Entropy>) -> std::io::Result<App> {
438	    Ok(App::open(disk, Schema::new(), entropy, AppConfig::default())?
439	        .mount_jobs(jobs![Charge, Mail])
440	        .outbound(Host::new("pay.test").bearer_env("PAY_KEY").max_reply_bytes(1 << 20))
441	        .outbound(Host::new("mail.test").header_env("X-Postmark-Server-Token", "POSTMARK_TOKEN"))
442	        .outbound_max_in_flight(64))
443	}
444	```
445	
446	The two methods have exactly these shapes. A `global` job's:
447	
448	```text
449	fn call(&self, tx: &Tx, key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError>
450	fn settle(self, tx: &mut Tx, reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError>
451	```
452	
453	A `scoped_by = Org` job's take its tenant's `ScopedTx`, as its `run` would:
454	
455	```text
456	fn call(&self, tx: &ScopedTx<'_, '_, Org>, key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError>
457	fn settle(self, tx: &mut ScopedTx<'_, '_, Org>, reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError>
458	```
459	
460	`call` takes a shared `&Tx`, so it reads and cannot write: a `tx.put` inside it is
461	a compile error, and so is a scoped job's `call` or `settle` taking a bare `Tx`
462	(§9 lists both). Whatever the call's outcome should change, `settle` writes. When
463	there is nothing to call any more (the order was cancelled after the enqueue, say),
464	`call` returns `Ok(None)`, and the job is done without a call.
465	
466	`key` is the job's idempotency key. The platform mints it when the job is
467	enqueued, 16 bytes from the node's entropy rendered as 32 lowercase hex
468	characters, and it stays the same across every retry and every re-dispatch after
469	a crash or a failover. charpente sends it nowhere by itself: `call` places it
470	where the remote reads one, the `idempotency-key` header above or a field of the
471	body, so a remote that honours it applies a repeated request once. It is not
472	`enqueue_keyed`'s app key.
473	
474	The minted key belongs to one job and covers that job's retries and
475	re-dispatches. An effect the app may enqueue more than once, a redrive after
476	Dead or a re-issued step, is a new job with a new key. So its `call` must send
477	an id of the effect itself, a field of the payload, or a remote that honours
478	keys applies the effect twice. Platform support for a re-issued job that keeps
479	its effect's key is planned for 0.5.0 (PLAN).
480	
481	Because the key is drawn as the enqueue is staged, an outbound job is enqueued
482	only in a transaction the platform opens: a route's, a job's or a cron tick's.
483	`Db::transact` and `Db::begin_group` (§4) cannot mint, and an outbound enqueue
484	inside either panics with a contract message (§9). Code that opens its own group
485	stages through `Db::begin_group_minting` instead, and a test seeds an outbound job
486	through `App::transact_for_tests`, which the message names.
487	
488	The request is built on the declared host, which is never runtime data:
489	`Call::get`, `post`, `put`, `patch` and `delete` take a path that begins with `/`.
490	`.header(name, value)` sends the name lowercase. `.json(&value)` and
491	`.form(&[(name, value)])` set the body and its `content-type`, and `.body(bytes)`
492	sets a raw body with none. A call carries one `content-type`, so setting another
493	(through `json`, `form` or `header`) replaces the earlier one. `settle` receives
494	the reply of any status, a 3xx included, since a redirect is never followed:
495	`reply.status()`, `reply.header(name)` (the first of that name, case-insensitively),
496	`reply.body()`, and `reply.json::<T>()`, which is a `JobError::App` when the body is
497	not `T`'s JSON.
498	
499	The host is a bare DNS name like `api.stripe.com`. A scheme, port, path or
500	userinfo in it is a compile error, because where the host resolves is the
501	operator's to say. `timeout` bounds the wait for the remote's reply, with
502	`backoff`'s syntax; it defaults to 30 s, and it is refused on a job without
503	`outbound`. `cross_tenant` beside `outbound` is refused: an outbound call runs in
504	the one tenant its job was enqueued in. An outbound job's `impl` that has `run`
505	instead of `call` and `settle` fails to compile too. §9 lists each refusal's
506	text.
507	
508	Outbound-ness is part of a job's shape: an outbound job's `FINGERPRINT` continues
509	its fingerprint as a pure job (`charpente::core::db::outbound_fingerprint`), so
510	adding `outbound` to a job, or removing it, is a shape change. It is refused while
511	Pending jobs of the old shape exist, and the ways through are the two "Changing a
512	job's fields" below describes: drain first, or a new type. The host is not part of
513	the shape, so changing the host is not refused.
514	
515	`#[job]` writes a job's `OUTBOUND` constant and its mounted `JobDef.outbound` from
516	the one declaration, so the two agree. A hand-written `impl Job` or a hand-built
517	`JobDef` can make them disagree under the same shape, and dispatch routes a row by
518	whether its enqueue minted a key, so that row would reach a glue the mounted job does
519	not have. From `App::mount_jobs` on, such an enqueue refuses its whole transaction
520	before any key is drawn, and is answered the way the shape refusal in "Changing a
521	job's fields" below is. `<value>` is `true` or `false`, and `<declaration>` is
522	`a pure job` or `` `outbound = "<host>"` ``:
523	
524	<!-- pinned -->
525	```text
526	job "<job>" was enqueued with `OUTBOUND = <value>`, but this binary mounts <job> as <declaration> under the same shape (<shape>) — dispatch routes a row by whether its enqueue minted an idempotency key, which only an `OUTBOUND = true` enqueue does, so this row would reach a glue the mounted <job> does not have; a hand-written `impl Job` or `JobDef` contradicts <job>'s #[job]; the transaction was refused and nothing was written, so a retry cannot succeed — enqueue the mounted type, give the other type its own name, or mount <job> as its #[job] declares it (GUIDE §6)
527	```
528	
529	A row that already disagrees, enqueued by a binary that did not mount the name,
530	stops the kernel at dispatch with a `contract:` panic that names the job and the
531	fix, rather than spending its retries on a glue that cannot run.
532	
533	### Declaring the hosts
534	
535	An outbound job names its host; the `App` says how to reach it. Declare one
536	`Host` per host that a mounted job calls, as `build_app` at the end of the `Charge`
537	block above does.
538	
539	The builders are `bearer_env(var)`, `header_env(name, var)`, `basic_env(user_var,
540	pass_var)`, `max_request_bytes(n)` and `max_reply_bytes(n)`. A credential is the
541	NAME of an environment variable. `serve` reads each value once, when it starts
542	(as `serve_with`, `serve_replicated`, `backup` and `archive` do, §5), and the
543	value never enters the log, the sim, an error text or `describe`, which lists
544	variable and header names only. A variable that is unset, empty, holds a
545	control character or is not UTF-8 refuses the start before the listener is
546	bound (a `basic_env` pair included, though base64 would carry a control
547	character: one there is a pasted newline, not a credential). The one
548	exception is a `basic_env` password, which may be empty, since APIs that take
549	the key as the username (Stripe's `-u sk_…:`) send `user:`:
550	
551	<!-- pinned -->
552	```text
553	outbound: <var> is unset — host <host> needs it for job <job>
554	outbound: <var> is set but empty — host <host> needs it for job <job>
555	outbound: <var> holds a control character (a trailing newline, say) or is not UTF-8 — host <host> needs it for job <job>; set it to the credential alone
556	```
557	
558	`<job>` is the first mounted job that calls `<host>`. The caps default to
559	1 MiB and 4 MiB, and neither passes `MAX_CAP_BYTES` (8 MiB).
560	
561	Each host is reached at `https://<host>:443` over HTTP/1.1, its certificate
562	verified against Mozilla's root store (`webpki-roots`, so the answer does not
563	vary with the machine's OS). An operator moves the address with
564	`--outbound-base` and adds a CA with `--outbound-ca` (§5); neither changes the
565	name that TLS verifies. No redirect is followed, so a 3xx is a reply that
566	`settle` reads. The client neither retries nor times out on its own: both are
567	the kernel's, through `retry` and `timeout`.
568	
569	The two sets must match both ways, checked when the kernel is built, so mount
570	order is free. A called host with no entry is refused with
571	`kernel: job <job> calls <host>, which has no Host entry — add
572	app.outbound(Host::new("<host>")) with the credentials it needs (GUIDE §6)`,
573	and an entry no mounted job calls with `kernel:
574	app.outbound(Host::new("<host>")) declares a host no mounted job calls —
575	remove it, or mount the job that calls it`. Declaring one host twice panics
576	at `app.outbound`. `app.outbound_hosts()` returns the hosts the mounted jobs
577	call, sorted: the list `sim.outbound` takes.
578	
579	`app.outbound_max_in_flight(n)` sets how many calls a node keeps in flight at
580	once (default 64, `charpente::outbound::DEFAULT_MAX_IN_FLIGHT`). A due
581	outbound job waits while the table is full, and a pure job never waits behind
582	it.
583	
584	### When a call fails
585	
586	The kernel starts a call only after the transaction that ran `call` has
587	committed, so a call never goes out on state that did not become durable,
588	including a write by another job in the same batch that `call` read. It waits
589	for the reply outside any transaction, for at most `timeout`, and hands the
590	reply to `settle`. An attempt below counts against `retry` the way a failed
591	`run` does: `attempts` increments, `last_error` names the failure, and the job
592	waits out its backoff or goes Dead. Every retry carries the job's key unchanged.
593	
594	| What happens | An attempt? | Result |
595	|---|---|---|
596	| `call` returns `Ok(None)` | — | Done; no call |
597	| `call` returns `Err(JobError::App)` or panics (`call panicked: …`) | yes | failure record; no call |
598	| `call` builds a request its `Host` entry refuses | yes | failure record naming the rule; no call |
599	| `call` returns `Err(JobError::Io)` | no | bubbles: restart-and-recover |
600	| a transport failure: refused, TLS, DNS, a reset, a reply over the cap | yes | failure record |
601	| `timeout` passes with no reply | yes | the call is cancelled; failure record |
602	| a reply for a call that already timed out or was dropped | — | discarded, counted in `outbound_late` |
603	| `settle` returns `Ok` | — | its writes and the Done mark commit as one record |
604	| `settle` returns `Err(JobError::App)` or panics (`settle panicked: …`) | yes | its writes discarded; failure record |
605	| `settle` returns `Err(JobError::Io)` | no | bubbles; still Pending, called again after the restart |
606	| the process crashes with calls in flight | no | the Pending jobs are called again on restart |
607	| the node stops being writable (a switchover, a demotion) | no | its calls in flight are dropped; the next writable node calls again |
608	| the node is restored from its archive | no | Pending rows keep their key, so a re-call is the same request |
609	
610	An attempt that may have reached the remote says so. Only a refused connection
611	certainly did not, so it is the one text that says the call never arrived:
612	
613	<!-- pinned -->
614	```text
615	outbound <host>: <error> — the call did not reach the remote
616	outbound <host>: <error> — the remote may have applied this call; the retry carries the same idempotency key
617	outbound <host>: timed out after <timeout> — the remote may have applied this call; the retry carries the same idempotency key

622	sent: a refused connection, a failed DNS lookup or a failed TLS handshake. Its
623	`<error>` names which: `connection refused` in the sim, and in production

625	tcp connect error: Connection refused (os error 61)`, say), or `the outbound
626	runtime thread is gone` for a call the client's dead thread never took. The second is

628	job's `timeout` as Rust prints a `Duration` (`2s`, `1.5s`), and `<cap>` is the
629	host's reply cap in bytes.

632	remote: a call whose reply was lost, or that timed out, may have been applied
633	there. The Dead job's `last_error` says which of the texts above ended it.

635	**A remote that ignores the key is called again, and may bill again.** A retry
636	after a lost reply or a timeout sends the same request with the same key. A

642	**A crash-looping process calls again on every restart.** A crash is not an

669	use charpente::kernel::{Kernel, SimSource};

let drive = Drive::new(sim, build_app); // build_app: Fn(&Sim) -> io::Result<App>
let phase = drive.faulted_phase(&requests, Duration::from_secs(2))?; // steps 1 and 2
calm.store(true, Ordering::Relaxed); // a remote model's own switch stays yours
let Some(recovered) = drive.recover(&phase, Duration::from_secs(60))? else {
    return Ok(()); // given up by name

let snap = recovered.kernel.app().db().snapshot().map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;

1. **Boot through fallout.** `faulted_phase` boots the app with
   `boot_through_fallout` (below), up to eight boots, restarting between
   them as a supervisor would. A first boot that never gets past fault
   fallout is no give-up: the phase is empty, and `recover` sends
   everything. In every step, fault fallout means `is_fault_fallout(t) ||
   clock_fallout(sim, t)`.
2. **A faulted phase.** The requests, each an offset from the instant the app
   booted and in arrival order, run through one kernel under the run's faults
   until nothing is left inside the horizon. An offset past the horizon
   panics before anything runs, since the phase would never send that
   request, naming the last offset, the horizon and the fix: raise the
   horizon past the last request, or space the requests closer. An offset
   equal to the horizon is sent. The kernel gets the sim's
   outbound handle exactly when the app declares hosts. Fault fallout ends
   the phase: it is the crash under test, never a give-up and never a skip,
   and the answers already recorded stand. `phase.answers[i]` is request
   `i`'s `(status, body)`, or `None` when it went unanswered;
   `phase.status(i)` is its status.
3. **A fault-free tail.** `recover` power-cycles (`sim.restart()`),
   quiesces the disk and clock faults, and the outbound faults when the app
   declares hosts. It waits out a clock refusal, boots, and runs the kernel to
   `tail` past the instant it booted, so due jobs, retries and cron drain. A
   remote model's own switches, such as `modelled_remote`'s `calm`, stay in
   your code: flip them between the two calls.
4. **Re-send what went unanswered.** Every request whose answer is `None`,
   or a 5xx whose body is fault fallout, is sent again at the tail's start. A
   4xx, or a handler's own 5xx, is the app's answer and is not re-sent.
   Fallout is read from the body's text (`is_fault_fallout`), so a handler's
   own 5xx whose message reads as fallout ("injected", say) is re-sent too.
   The re-sent answers come back in `recovered.resent`, apart from the
   phase's, because a request that went unanswered may or may not have
   landed. So a claim about acked requests reads `phase.status(i) ==
   Some(200)`, and a check that wants the two merged merges them itself
   (`examples/drawn_inputs.rs`).

**A route the tail re-sends must be safe to receive twice.** `Drive`
re-sends, and a request that went unanswered may have landed, so its re-send
is the second delivery a production client's retry makes. Answer a repeat of
the same request with what the first one did, and change nothing:
`modelled_remote`'s `place_order` answers an order that is already stored, and
the scaffold's `add_note` a note already stored with the same body. A request
that reuses the id with other content is a
conflict, not a repeat: refuse it with a 4xx that names the conflict and the
fix, as `add_note` does for a note that already holds another body. A route
that fails this is an app defect the re-send found, and its check goes red
with a seed. Fix the route: dropping below the helper to skip the re-send
hides the defect.

`recover` gives `Ok(None)` when the run gave up by name, on a boot refused for
durable corruption and on nothing else. Return `Ok(())` then. Its errors fail
the run:

- `the fault-free tail could not boot`: every boot met fault fallout, and
  nothing gave the run up.
- `the boot was refused for the clock a third time, after two waits past the
  instant each refusal named. …, so this is a platform clock defect, not the
  app's: report it with this run's seed. The third refusal: the fault-free tail
  could not boot: <refusal>`, from `wait_out_clock_refusal`. One wait always
  suffices, so a refusal that outlasts two is a charpente defect, and the run
  fails on it rather than hiding it as a skip.
- `the fault-free tail could not boot: <error>`: a boot, or the kernel's
  build, failed with an error of its own.
- `the fault-free tail's kernel stopped: <error>`, in the kernel's words.
- `the app calls <host>, but the workload registered no model for it — call
  sim.remote("<host>", …) before Drive::faulted_phase`, from either call.

**When to drop below the helper.** `Drive` is one faulted phase and one tail.
A workload with more than that builds it from the pieces this section and
"Driving the whole app in a sim" describe: `boot_through_fallout`,
`Kernel::new` or `Kernel::with_outbound` over a `SimSource`, the quiesce calls
below and `wait_out_clock_refusal`. Examples are several faulted rounds, a
supervisor loop inside the phase, a script that reads one phase's answers to
build the next, several nodes, a check between the phase and the tail, and a
check that reads the frames an SSE subscriber received (`source.sinks()`):
`Drive` hands back neither phase's source, so it exposes no frames. §11's
"Testing a tail in sim" builds its source by hand to read them. A route that
cannot take the re-send is not a reason to drop below it: fix the route
(above). Keep each step's rule as `Drive` has it:
- use the fallout filter in every step;
- treat a crash in the faulted phase as the crash under test, not a skip;
- quiesce before the tail boots, and wait out a clock refusal;
- give up only on a durable refusal;
- re-send in the tail what went unanswered, to routes safe to receive twice.

A check that runs at the end of a run — a checkpoint, a graceful close, a
byte comparison of two nodes' files — does IO, and the run's
`FaultConfig` still applies to it. "No fault has fired so far" is a fact about
the past: the check's own fsync can still draw an injected failure. Call
`sim.quiesce_disk_faults()` first. For the rest of the run, on every disk,
it disarms any pending crash countdown, and no injected read, write, sync or
directory-barrier error, misdirected write or restart bit flip fires after it.
Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a run that never calls it
replays exactly as before. After it, an error in the check is a real failure,
not fallout to classify. Network and object-store faults are untouched, and a
restart still power-cycles: unsynced writes and directory entries collapse under
the crash model as usual (`crash_apply`, `crash_torn`, `dir_entry_loss`).

An outbound workload's tail needs the outbound half as well.
`sim.quiesce_outbound_faults()` ends the five outbound fault axes for the rest of
the run: no call started after it is refused, lost, throttled or slowed, or
loses its reply. Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a run that never calls
it replays exactly as before. Latency stays, since it is not a fault, and a
request already in flight keeps the fate it drew. Call both, then run past the
last backoff and deadline. From there every call reaches its remote and its
reply comes back, so every outbound job settles or retries to Dead, which is
what `outbound_settles_by_horizon` (below) checks.

A realtime workload's settle phase has the same need for a different fault. The
subscriber-stall rate is the one fault axis the sim does not inject itself: a
workload reads `sim.subscriber_stall()` and drives its own sink's stall closure
at that rate. `sim.quiesce_subscriber_stalls()` makes that accessor read 0.0 for
the rest of the run, so a stall closure built after it never refuses a send
and draws nothing. Call it before a phase whose verdict rests on a delivery
completing. A stall there is a fault the property excuses, so a stall that drops
the only clean attempt's tail leaves the run with no verdict at all.

A tail that opens a kernel needs the clock half too.
`sim.quiesce_clock_faults()` ends the clock faults ("Wall time and its faults",
below) for the rest of the run, on every clock. No reading steps back and
no power cycle jumps a clock forward after it, so each clock's offset stays
where the run left it, skew included. Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a
run that never calls it replays exactly as before. It does not undo the
past: a step back in an earlier phase can leave the clock more than the
tolerance behind the latest time the store recorded, and then the tail's open is
refused (§7). With the offset frozen, the clock reaches the instant the refusal
names as virtual time passes. `clock_reopens_after(text)` (below) reads that
instant. Sleep a little past it (`sim.clock().sleep(…)`), restart the process (a
refused node exits, and its supervisor starts it again), and boot again. One
wait is enough, since nothing moves the clock or the recorded time in between.
Bound the loop anyway, and fail the run by name once the bound is spent: no
injected fault explains a refusal one wait did not clear, so it is a platform
defect, and a skip would hide it. `wait_out_clock_refusal(sim, boot)` (below)
is that loop, and `Drive::recover` runs it around the tail's boot.

### Restarting the process, not the machine

`sim.restart()` is a power cycle: every unsynced write survives, tears or
vanishes before anything reopens. Most restarts in production are not that. A
supervisor restarting a crashed, killed or exited process finds the OS page
cache intact: every write the dead process made is still readable, synced or
not. `sim.restart_process()` models that. Every open file handle dies, exactly
as after `restart`, and nothing else happens. Unsynced writes and directory
entries stay pending and readable, and the next `restart()` still collapses
them.

The difference matters because readable is not durable. A node that reads back
what a dead process wrote and persists anything derived from it, before making
it durable, has built on data the next power loss can take away. A store
outran its own log exactly that way: recovery replayed a WAL frame whose fsync
had failed, the store checkpointed past it, and a power cycle dropped the frame.
Charpente now syncs what it reads back at boot before it acts on it. A property
that only ever power-cycles cannot reach that shape. One that mixes the two can.

The sim's kernel is an honest one: a failed sync leaves its writes pending, and
the next sync writes them. On Linux a failed fsync can instead mark the pages
clean, so the bytes stay readable and never reach the disk. No restart mode
models that, and no later sync can repair it.

Call `restart_process()` before you drop the old process's `Db` to model a kill:
its open files are dead, so nothing it flushes through them on the way out
reaches the disk. Only file handles are gated. A destructor that opens a file
afresh through a `Disk` it still holds would reach the disk; charpente's own
close goes through its open files. Call it after the drop to model an exit.

`sim.unsynced_files()` lists the files that hold writes no sync has taken yet.
Read it right after `restart_process()` to prove the restart left the next
process something unsynced to read back. A property that marks "read back an
unsynced write" from that list cannot be satisfied by a restart that quietly
flushed.

`restart_process()` draws from no random stream and clears no crash countdown,
so the sim gained it without re-keying anyone's runs. Calling it does
change everything your workload does afterwards, as any restart would. It marks
`restart:process`, never `restart`. A crashed disk is power loss, and
`restart_process()` refuses it by name: call `restart()` there. It covers the
global disk; hosts have no process restart.

### Wall time and its faults

A workload reads two times. `sim.now()` is virtual time, the one dimension every
host shares; `SimSource` horizons and `push_at` times are on it. A clock's
`wall()` (`sim.clock()`, or a host's `host.clock()`) is the wall time a node
sees: `sim.true_wall()` (virtual time plus 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z) plus that
clock's offset. `charpente test --sim` puts three faults on the offset, each on
in a quarter of runs, from its own stream:

| Axis (`FaultConfig` field) | What it does | Coverage key |
|---|---|---|
| `clock_skew` | the run's largest skew, up to 120 s: each clock draws its own skew once, uniform within ±`clock_skew`, and reads that far ahead (+) or behind (-) of true time | `clock:skewed`, once per clock, at its first read |
| `clock_step_back` | per wall read, the chance the clock steps back by up to 120 s, and stays there | `clock:stepped-back` per step, and `clock:stepped-back:within-tolerance` or `clock:stepped-back:beyond-tolerance` by its size against `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` |
| `clock_downtime` | per power cycle (`sim.restart()`, `host.restart()`), the chance the clock jumps forward by up to three days, as if the machine had been off; virtual time stays put, and `restart_process()` is not downtime | `clock:downtime`, per jump, at the first reading that shows it |

Each clock's skew, step-backs and jumps are its own, so two hosts' clocks
disagree from their first read. The faults compound. A clock's offset is its
skew plus every step back and jump it has taken so far, and nothing pulls it
back toward true time, just as a clock with no NTP keeps its error, so the
offset wanders further as a run goes on. `sim.clock().offset()` (or
`host.clock().offset()`) reports it at any moment and draws nothing.
The sizes span both sides of `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` (60 s), so a run sees what a node
does with a bad clock (§5, §7): it holds its wall reading at the latest time it
used for a step back within the tolerance, stops by name for one beyond it
(`clock went backwards: …`) or for a hold that lasts longer than the tolerance
(`clock stalled: …`), and refuses to open while its clock is more than the
tolerance behind the latest time its data directory recorded (`refusing to
open: this node's wall clock …`). `clock_refused` names the stops and the
refusal (below). They are fallout only where a clock fault acted:
`clock_fallout(sim, text)` excuses one once a clock in this run has read with
its own skew, stepped back, or shown a jump, and `is_fault_fallout` alone never
does. A node whose clock is right is refused only by a bug, and the platform's
suites run with the clock axes off, so a refusal there fails. An app workload's
filter is `|t| is_fault_fallout(t) || clock_fallout(sim, t)`. The fault-free
tail above quiesces the clock and then waits out a refusal.

A property that judges expiry and lateness judges two things. Against each
node's own clock readings it holds the node to what it promises (below), which
is exact. Against `sim.true_wall()` it states what that promise means in true
time, written through each clock's offset, since a skewed clock is the thing
under test and a bound that assumes the node's reading is true time fails on
correct code. The platform's own suites (`run_universes_swarm!`, `Sim::new`,
`FaultConfig::default()` and `none()`) leave the three axes off; a platform
property turns them on in `run_universes_swarm_with!`'s `adjust`, which is
handed the run's seed with its config (`|seed, cfg| …`), so any value it
draws comes from a stream keyed by that seed.

`tests/clock.rs` in the `charpente` crate (`crates/charpente/tests/clock.rs` in
a checkout) is the worked example. It runs four platform properties with all
three axes on (sessions, a one-second schedule, retries, and the stops and
refusals themselves, on one node and on a follower promoted on its own host's
clock) and a victim clock that fails two of them by name. It shows how to write
the bounds.

Write a bound through each clock's offset, the reading minus `sim.true_wall()`
at that instant, never through `clock_skew`. A step back within the tolerance
is held and then caught up, so step-backs add up, and a clock can run any
distance behind true time without a check firing. A bound on `expires_at` that
allows only the skew fails on correct code.

What a node does guarantee is relative to its own clock. The time it hands out
is never behind its clock's reading, and never more than `CLOCK_TOLERANCE`
ahead of it: the hold takes the larger, the stop fires past the tolerance, and
the open refuses past it. Nor does it stay ahead for longer than the tolerance
at a stretch, since the stall stop ends the hold. That gives these bounds:
- A session resolves only while the clock judging it reads before its
  `expires_at`. In true time, it resolves no later than its TTL plus the
  tolerance after it was minted, plus however far the judging clock has fallen
  behind the minting one.
- A schedule never sits idle once its slot has come on the node's clock.
- Two ticks are never further apart in true time than one interval plus the
  tolerance, plus the clock's own loss and the time the node was busy.

The file records every wall read the kernel makes (a `Clock` wrapper around
`sim.clock()`) and steps the kernel by hand. That ties each response, tick and
retry to the reading it was decided at.

### The checkers

`charpente_sim::checks` ships seventeen functions: twelve reusable oracles, two
typed event reads, and three idioms, one for a boot and two for a tail that waits out a clock
refusal. Reach for these before hand-rolling the same logic a fourth time:

- `is_fault_fallout(text: &str) -> bool` — classifies an error's *text*:
  is this the harness's own injected fault (or its consequences) rather
  than a bug your workload should fail on? It recognizes the sim's
  injected-fault wording (including the `read_error` axis), the WAL/engine
  poison wording, and redb's "close and re-open the database" latch. Used
  inside a workload to turn "the disk broke, as instructed" into "no answer
  this round" rather than a hard failure — never to swallow anything else.
  (`misdirected_write` is not in that list and cannot be: it returns `Ok`, so
  it has no wording — what you eventually see is the corrupt frame it left
  behind.) **It never excuses the WAL's durable-horizon refusal**, the boot
  refused because an already-acknowledged frame failed its check at or below
  the store's horizon. That refusal is fallout where `bit_flip` or
  `misdirected_write` fired, and a durability bug in the platform everywhere
  else (a real one showed itself only as this refusal in 8 of 21 failing
  bases), and text cannot say which. So it is `false` here, and an open site
  asks `durable_refusal` (below) first, or, for one node of several,
  `SimHost::durable_corruption_fired()`. `boot_through_fallout` does that for
  you. **Nor does it excuse the kernel's clock stops or open/promote refusal**,
  for the same reason: a clock fault or a platform bug produces it, and
  `clock_fallout` (below) tells them apart.
- `classify(text: &str) -> FaultReason` — the families, typed:
  `Injected`, `Poisoned`, `RedbLatch`, `DurableHorizon`, `ClockRefused`, or
  `Unrelated` (`is_fault_fallout` is `Injected | Poisoned | RedbLatch`). Use it when your
  workload wants to accept some families and fail on others — e.g. "an
  injected fault is fallout this round, but a poisoned engine is a finding" —
  or to name the family in a coverage key. `DurableHorizon` and
  `ClockRefused` are names, never excuses on their own. Matching on a variant instead of on substrings keeps
  the prose coupling in one place: if a platform error string is ever
  reworded, `classify` is the single site that must change, and it fails by
  name instead of leaking a wrong classification into whichever oracle saw
  the text first.
- `clock_refused(text: &str) -> bool` — true for the kernel's clock stops
  (`clock went backwards: …`, `clock stalled: …`) and for its refusal to open or promote a node
  whose wall clock is more than `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` behind the latest time its
  data directory recorded (`refusing to open: this node's wall clock …`,
  `refusing to promote: this node's wall clock …`). A name only: the clock
  axes produce both ("Wall time and its faults", above), and so does a
  platform bug that refuses a node whose clock is right.
- `clock_fallout(sim: &Sim, text: &str) -> bool` — the excuse for those:
  true when `clock_refused(text)` holds and a clock fault acted in this run (a
  clock read with its own skew, stepped back, or showed a downtime jump: its
  `clock:*` coverage key fired). Where no clock fault acted, nothing excuses
  the stops or the refusal. An app workload that runs a kernel filters fallout
  with `|t| is_fault_fallout(t) || clock_fallout(sim, t)`; a workload that
  never builds a kernel cannot see either text.
- `clock_reopens_after(text: &str) -> Option<WallTime>` — the instant a clock
  stop or refusal names as the one after which the node runs again (its final
  "after <instant>", to the millisecond), or `None` for any other text. A
  fault-free tail sleeps a little past it after `sim.quiesce_clock_faults()`,
  restarts the process and boots again ("A fault-free tail", above). The stall
  stop names no instant, so it is `None`: its clock stopped advancing, and no
  wait fixes that. A quiesced clock still advances, so a tail's kernel never
  stalls, and one that does is reported rather than waited out.
- `wait_out_clock_refusal(sim: &Sim, boot: impl FnMut() -> Result<Option<T>, String>) -> Result<Option<T>, String>`
  — that wait, as a loop. It calls `boot` (your boot and kernel, returning
  `Ok(Some(_))` once booted, `Ok(None)` when it gave the run up, and the error's
  text otherwise) and returns what it returns, unless the error is a clock stop
  or refusal that `clock_fallout` excuses and that names an instant. Then it
  sleeps one second past that instant, restarts the process, and calls `boot`
  again, twice at most: a third refusal is an `Err` that fails the run, `the
  boot was refused for the clock a third time, … a platform clock defect, not
  the app's: report it with this run's seed. The third refusal: <refusal>`,
  and never a give-up. Any other error, the stall stop included, comes back
  unchanged. Call it after `sim.quiesce_clock_faults()`; `Drive::recover`
  runs it around the tail's boot, so only a workload below the helper calls
  it.
- `replays_identically(seed: u64, workload: impl Fn(&mut Sim) -> Result<T, String>) -> Result<(), String>`
  — the determinism oracle. Runs `workload` twice, each on its own fresh
  `Sim::new(seed)`, and fails if the returned value or the durable
  end-state (`Sim::durable_fingerprint`) diverge. It always constructs
  plain `Sim::new` worlds — never a *swarm* `FaultConfig` (swarm testing:
  the harness samples each run's fault rates and latency ranges from
  its own seed, so a batch explores many fault mixes instead of every
  run sharing one fixed matrix) — so it re-runs the workload's logic
  under default fault rates rather than replaying the exact fault schedule

  worlds identical at time zero**, which a sim that has already run cannot give

- `acked_implies_durable(sim: &mut Sim, rounds: u32, drive: impl FnMut(&mut Sim) -> Result<Vec<String>, String>, verify: impl FnMut(&mut Sim, &[String]) -> Result<(), String>) -> Result<(), String>`

- `durable_corruption_fired(sim: &Sim) -> bool` — true when a

tool_use_result.stdout:
```text
let drive = Drive::new(sim, build_app); // build_app: Fn(&Sim) -> io::Result<App>
let phase = drive.faulted_phase(&requests, Duration::from_secs(2))?; // steps 1 and 2
calm.store(true, Ordering::Relaxed); // a remote model's own switch stays yours
let Some(recovered) = drive.recover(&phase, Duration::from_secs(60))? else {
    return Ok(()); // given up by name
}; // steps 3 and 4
let snap = recovered.kernel.app().db().snapshot().map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
```

1. **Boot through fallout.** `faulted_phase` boots the app with
   `boot_through_fallout` (below), up to eight boots, restarting between
   them as a supervisor would. A first boot that never gets past fault
   fallout is no give-up: the phase is empty, and `recover` sends
   everything. In every step, fault fallout means `is_fault_fallout(t) ||
   clock_fallout(sim, t)`.
2. **A faulted phase.** The requests, each an offset from the instant the app
   booted and in arrival order, run through one kernel under the run's faults
   until nothing is left inside the horizon. An offset past the horizon
   panics before anything runs, since the phase would never send that
   request, naming the last offset, the horizon and the fix: raise the
   horizon past the last request, or space the requests closer. An offset
   equal to the horizon is sent. The kernel gets the sim's
   outbound handle exactly when the app declares hosts. Fault fallout ends
   the phase: it is the crash under test, never a give-up and never a skip,
   and the answers already recorded stand. `phase.answers[i]` is request
   `i`'s `(status, body)`, or `None` when it went unanswered;
   `phase.status(i)` is its status.
3. **A fault-free tail.** `recover` power-cycles (`sim.restart()`),
   quiesces the disk and clock faults, and the outbound faults when the app
   declares hosts. It waits out a clock refusal, boots, and runs the kernel to
   `tail` past the instant it booted, so due jobs, retries and cron drain. A
   remote model's own switches, such as `modelled_remote`'s `calm`, stay in
   your code: flip them between the two calls.
4. **Re-send what went unanswered.** Every request whose answer is `None`,
   or a 5xx whose body is fault fallout, is sent again at the tail's start. A
   4xx, or a handler's own 5xx, is the app's answer and is not re-sent.
   Fallout is read from the body's text (`is_fault_fallout`), so a handler's
   own 5xx whose message reads as fallout ("injected", say) is re-sent too.
   The re-sent answers come back in `recovered.resent`, apart from the
   phase's, because a request that went unanswered may or may not have
   landed. So a claim about acked requests reads `phase.status(i) ==
   Some(200)`, and a check that wants the two merged merges them itself
   (`examples/drawn_inputs.rs`).

**A route the tail re-sends must be safe to receive twice.** `Drive`
re-sends, and a request that went unanswered may have landed, so its re-send
is the second delivery a production client's retry makes. Answer a repeat of
the same request with what the first one did, and change nothing:
`modelled_remote`'s `place_order` answers an order that is already stored, and
the scaffold's `add_note` a note already stored with the same body. A request
that reuses the id with other content is a
conflict, not a repeat: refuse it with a 4xx that names the conflict and the
fix, as `add_note` does for a note that already holds another body. A route
that fails this is an app defect the re-send found, and its check goes red
with a seed. Fix the route: dropping below the helper to skip the re-send
hides the defect.

`recover` gives `Ok(None)` when the run gave up by name, on a boot refused for
durable corruption and on nothing else. Return `Ok(())` then. Its errors fail
the run:

- `the fault-free tail could not boot`: every boot met fault fallout, and
  nothing gave the run up.
- `the boot was refused for the clock a third time, after two waits past the
  instant each refusal named. …, so this is a platform clock defect, not the
  app's: report it with this run's seed. The third refusal: the fault-free tail
  could not boot: <refusal>`, from `wait_out_clock_refusal`. One wait always
  suffices, so a refusal that outlasts two is a charpente defect, and the run
  fails on it rather than hiding it as a skip.
- `the fault-free tail could not boot: <error>`: a boot, or the kernel's
  build, failed with an error of its own.
- `the fault-free tail's kernel stopped: <error>`, in the kernel's words.
- `the app calls <host>, but the workload registered no model for it — call
  sim.remote("<host>", …) before Drive::faulted_phase`, from either call.

**When to drop below the helper.** `Drive` is one faulted phase and one tail.
A workload with more than that builds it from the pieces this section and
"Driving the whole app in a sim" describe: `boot_through_fallout`,
`Kernel::new` or `Kernel::with_outbound` over a `SimSource`, the quiesce calls
below and `wait_out_clock_refusal`. Examples are several faulted rounds, a
supervisor loop inside the phase, a script that reads one phase's answers to
build the next, several nodes, a check between the phase and the tail, and a
check that reads the frames an SSE subscriber received (`source.sinks()`):
`Drive` hands back neither phase's source, so it exposes no frames. §11's
"Testing a tail in sim" builds its source by hand to read them. A route that
cannot take the re-send is not a reason to drop below it: fix the route
(above). Keep each step's rule as `Drive` has it:
- use the fallout filter in every step;
- treat a crash in the faulted phase as the crash under test, not a skip;
- quiesce before the tail boots, and wait out a clock refusal;
- give up only on a durable refusal;
- re-send in the tail what went unanswered, to routes safe to receive twice.

A check that runs at the end of a run — a checkpoint, a graceful close, a
byte comparison of two nodes' files — does IO, and the run's
`FaultConfig` still applies to it. "No fault has fired so far" is a fact about
the past: the check's own fsync can still draw an injected failure. Call
`sim.quiesce_disk_faults()` first. For the rest of the run, on every disk,
it disarms any pending crash countdown, and no injected read, write, sync or
directory-barrier error, misdirected write or restart bit flip fires after it.
Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a run that never calls it
replays exactly as before. After it, an error in the check is a real failure,
not fallout to classify. Network and object-store faults are untouched, and a
restart still power-cycles: unsynced writes and directory entries collapse under
the crash model as usual (`crash_apply`, `crash_torn`, `dir_entry_loss`).

An outbound workload's tail needs the outbound half as well.
`sim.quiesce_outbound_faults()` ends the five outbound fault axes for the rest of
the run: no call started after it is refused, lost, throttled or slowed, or
loses its reply. Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a run that never calls
it replays exactly as before. Latency stays, since it is not a fault, and a
request already in flight keeps the fate it drew. Call both, then run past the
last backoff and deadline. From there every call reaches its remote and its
reply comes back, so every outbound job settles or retries to Dead, which is
what `outbound_settles_by_horizon` (below) checks.

A realtime workload's settle phase has the same need for a different fault. The
subscriber-stall rate is the one fault axis the sim does not inject itself: a
workload reads `sim.subscriber_stall()` and drives its own sink's stall closure
at that rate. `sim.quiesce_subscriber_stalls()` makes that accessor read 0.0 for
the rest of the run, so a stall closure built after it never refuses a send
and draws nothing. Call it before a phase whose verdict rests on a delivery
completing. A stall there is a fault the property excuses, so a stall that drops
the only clean attempt's tail leaves the run with no verdict at all.

A tail that opens a kernel needs the clock half too.
`sim.quiesce_clock_faults()` ends the clock faults ("Wall time and its faults",
below) for the rest of the run, on every clock. No reading steps back and
no power cycle jumps a clock forward after it, so each clock's offset stays
where the run left it, skew included. Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a
run that never calls it replays exactly as before. It does not undo the
past: a step back in an earlier phase can leave the clock more than the
tolerance behind the latest time the store recorded, and then the tail's open is
refused (§7). With the offset frozen, the clock reaches the instant the refusal
names as virtual time passes. `clock_reopens_after(text)` (below) reads that
instant. Sleep a little past it (`sim.clock().sleep(…)`), restart the process (a
refused node exits, and its supervisor starts it again), and boot again. One
wait is enough, since nothing moves the clock or the recorded time in between.
Bound the loop anyway, and fail the run by name once the bound is spent: no
injected fault explains a refusal one wait did not clear, so it is a platform
defect, and a skip would hide it. `wait_out_clock_refusal(sim, boot)` (below)
is that loop, and `Drive::recover` runs it around the tail's boot.

### Restarting the process, not the machine

`sim.restart()` is a power cycle: every unsynced write survives, tears or
vanishes before anything reopens. Most restarts in production are not that. A
supervisor restarting a crashed, killed or exited process finds the OS page
cache intact: every write the dead process made is still readable, synced or
not. `sim.restart_process()` models that. Every open file handle dies, exactly
as after `restart`, and nothing else happens. Unsynced writes and directory
entries stay pending and readable, and the next `restart()` still collapses
them.

The difference matters because readable is not durable. A node that reads back
what a dead process wrote and persists anything derived from it, before making
it durable, has built on data the next power loss can take away. A store
outran its own log exactly that way: recovery replayed a WAL frame whose fsync
had failed, the store checkpointed past it, and a power cycle dropped the frame.
Charpente now syncs what it reads back at boot before it acts on it. A property
that only ever power-cycles cannot reach that shape. One that mixes the two can.

The sim's kernel is an honest one: a failed sync leaves its writes pending, and
the next sync writes them. On Linux a failed fsync can instead mark the pages
clean, so the bytes stay readable and never reach the disk. No restart mode
models that, and no later sync can repair it.

Call `restart_process()` before you drop the old process's `Db` to model a kill:
its open files are dead, so nothing it flushes through them on the way out
reaches the disk. Only file handles are gated. A destructor that opens a file
afresh through a `Disk` it still holds would reach the disk; charpente's own
close goes through its open files. Call it after the drop to model an exit.

`sim.unsynced_files()` lists the files that hold writes no sync has taken yet.
Read it right after `restart_process()` to prove the restart left the next
process something unsynced to read back. A property that marks "read back an
unsynced write" from that list cannot be satisfied by a restart that quietly
flushed.

`restart_process()` draws from no random stream and clears no crash countdown,
so the sim gained it without re-keying anyone's runs. Calling it does
change everything your workload does afterwards, as any restart would. It marks
`restart:process`, never `restart`. A crashed disk is power loss, and
`restart_process()` refuses it by name: call `restart()` there. It covers the
global disk; hosts have no process restart.

### Wall time and its faults

A workload reads two times. `sim.now()` is virtual time, the one dimension every
host shares; `SimSource` horizons and `push_at` times are on it. A clock's
`wall()` (`sim.clock()`, or a host's `host.clock()`) is the wall time a node
sees: `sim.true_wall()` (virtual time plus 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z) plus that
clock's offset. `charpente test --sim` puts three faults on the offset, each on
in a quarter of runs, from its own stream:

| Axis (`FaultConfig` field) | What it does | Coverage key |
|---|---|---|
| `clock_skew` | the run's largest skew, up to 120 s: each clock draws its own skew once, uniform within ±`clock_skew`, and reads that far ahead (+) or behind (-) of true time | `clock:skewed`, once per clock, at its first read |
| `clock_step_back` | per wall read, the chance the clock steps back by up to 120 s, and stays there | `clock:stepped-back` per step, and `clock:stepped-back:within-tolerance` or `clock:stepped-back:beyond-tolerance` by its size against `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` |
| `clock_downtime` | per power cycle (`sim.restart()`, `host.restart()`), the chance the clock jumps forward by up to three days, as if the machine had been off; virtual time stays put, and `restart_process()` is not downtime | `clock:downtime`, per jump, at the first reading that shows it |

Each clock's skew, step-backs and jumps are its own, so two hosts' clocks
disagree from their first read. The faults compound. A clock's offset is its
skew plus every step back and jump it has taken so far, and nothing pulls it
back toward true time, just as a clock with no NTP keeps its error, so the
offset wanders further as a run goes on. `sim.clock().offset()` (or
`host.clock().offset()`) reports it at any moment and draws nothing.
The sizes span both sides of `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` (60 s), so a run sees what a node
does with a bad clock (§5, §7): it holds its wall reading at the latest time it
used for a step back within the tolerance, stops by name for one beyond it
(`clock went backwards: …`) or for a hold that lasts longer than the tolerance
(`clock stalled: …`), and refuses to open while its clock is more than the
tolerance behind the latest time its data directory recorded (`refusing to
open: this node's wall clock …`). `clock_refused` names the stops and the
refusal (below). They are fallout only where a clock fault acted:
`clock_fallout(sim, text)` excuses one once a clock in this run has read with
its own skew, stepped back, or shown a jump, and `is_fault_fallout` alone never
does. A node whose clock is right is refused only by a bug, and the platform's
suites run with the clock axes off, so a refusal there fails. An app workload's
filter is `|t| is_fault_fallout(t) || clock_fallout(sim, t)`. The fault-free
tail above quiesces the clock and then waits out a refusal.

A property that judges expiry and lateness judges two things. Against each
node's own clock readings it holds the node to what it promises (below), which
is exact. Against `sim.true_wall()` it states what that promise means in true
time, written through each clock's offset, since a skewed clock is the thing
under test and a bound that assumes the node's reading is true time fails on
correct code. The platform's own suites (`run_universes_swarm!`, `Sim::new`,
`FaultConfig::default()` and `none()`) leave the three axes off; a platform
property turns them on in `run_universes_swarm_with!`'s `adjust`, which is
handed the run's seed with its config (`|seed, cfg| …`), so any value it
draws comes from a stream keyed by that seed.

`tests/clock.rs` in the `charpente` crate (`crates/charpente/tests/clock.rs` in
a checkout) is the worked example. It runs four platform properties with all
three axes on (sessions, a one-second schedule, retries, and the stops and
refusals themselves, on one node and on a follower promoted on its own host's
clock) and a victim clock that fails two of them by name. It shows how to write
the bounds.

Write a bound through each clock's offset, the reading minus `sim.true_wall()`
at that instant, never through `clock_skew`. A step back within the tolerance
is held and then caught up, so step-backs add up, and a clock can run any
distance behind true time without a check firing. A bound on `expires_at` that
allows only the skew fails on correct code.

What a node does guarantee is relative to its own clock. The time it hands out
is never behind its clock's reading, and never more than `CLOCK_TOLERANCE`
ahead of it: the hold takes the larger, the stop fires past the tolerance, and
the open refuses past it. Nor does it stay ahead for longer than the tolerance
at a stretch, since the stall stop ends the hold. That gives these bounds:
- A session resolves only while the clock judging it reads before its
  `expires_at`. In true time, it resolves no later than its TTL plus the
  tolerance after it was minted, plus however far the judging clock has fallen
  behind the minting one.
- A schedule never sits idle once its slot has come on the node's clock.
- Two ticks are never further apart in true time than one interval plus the
  tolerance, plus the clock's own loss and the time the node was busy.

The file records every wall read the kernel makes (a `Clock` wrapper around
`sim.clock()`) and steps the kernel by hand. That ties each response, tick and
retry to the reading it was decided at.

### The checkers

`charpente_sim::checks` ships seventeen functions: twelve reusable oracles, two
typed event reads, and three idioms, one for a boot and two for a tail that waits out a clock
refusal. Reach for these before hand-rolling the same logic a fourth time:

- `is_fault_fallout(text: &str) -> bool` — classifies an error's *text*:
  is this the harness's own injected fault (or its consequences) rather
  than a bug your workload should fail on? It recognizes the sim's
  injected-fault wording (including the `read_error` axis), the WAL/engine
  poison wording, and redb's "close and re-open the database" latch. Used
  inside a workload to turn "the disk broke, as instructed" into "no answer
  this round" rather than a hard failure — never to swallow anything else.
  (`misdirected_write` is not in that list and cannot be: it returns `Ok`, so
  it has no wording — what you eventually see is the corrupt frame it left
  behind.) **It never excuses the WAL's durable-horizon refusal**, the boot
  refused because an already-acknowledged frame failed its check at or below
  the store's horizon. That refusal is fallout where `bit_flip` or
  `misdirected_write` fired, and a durability bug in the platform everywhere
  else (a real one showed itself only as this refusal in 8 of 21 failing
  bases), and text cannot say which. So it is `false` here, and an open site
  asks `durable_refusal` (below) first, or, for one node of several,
  `SimHost::durable_corruption_fired()`. `boot_through_fallout` does that for
  you. **Nor does it excuse the kernel's clock stops or open/promote refusal**,
  for the same reason: a clock fault or a platform bug produces it, and
  `clock_fallout` (below) tells them apart.
- `classify(text: &str) -> FaultReason` — the families, typed:
  `Injected`, `Poisoned`, `RedbLatch`, `DurableHorizon`, `ClockRefused`, or
  `Unrelated` (`is_fault_fallout` is `Injected | Poisoned | RedbLatch`). Use it when your
  workload wants to accept some families and fail on others — e.g. "an
  injected fault is fallout this round, but a poisoned engine is a finding" —
  or to name the family in a coverage key. `DurableHorizon` and
  `ClockRefused` are names, never excuses on their own. Matching on a variant instead of on substrings keeps
  the prose coupling in one place: if a platform error string is ever
  reworded, `classify` is the single site that must change, and it fails by
  name instead of leaking a wrong classification into whichever oracle saw
  the text first.
- `clock_refused(text: &str) -> bool` — true for the kernel's clock stops
  (`clock went backwards: …`, `clock stalled: …`) and for its refusal to open or promote a node
  whose wall clock is more than `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` behind the latest time its
  data directory recorded (`refusing to open: this node's wall clock …`,
  `refusing to promote: this node's wall clock …`). A name only: the clock
  axes produce both ("Wall time and its faults", above), and so does a
  platform bug that refuses a node whose clock is right.
- `clock_fallout(sim: &Sim, text: &str) -> bool` — the excuse for those:
  true when `clock_refused(text)` holds and a clock fault acted in this run (a
  clock read with its own skew, stepped back, or showed a downtime jump: its
  `clock:*` coverage key fired). Where no clock fault acted, nothing excuses
  the stops or the refusal. An app workload that runs a kernel filters fallout
  with `|t| is_fault_fallout(t) || clock_fallout(sim, t)`; a workload that
  never builds a kernel cannot see either text.
- `clock_reopens_after(text: &str) -> Option<WallTime>` — the instant a clock
  stop or refusal names as the one after which the node runs again (its final
  "after <instant>", to the millisecond), or `None` for any other text. A
  fault-free tail sleeps a little past it after `sim.quiesce_clock_faults()`,
  restarts the process and boots again ("A fault-free tail", above). The stall
  stop names no instant, so it is `None`: its clock stopped advancing, and no
  wait fixes that. A quiesced clock still advances, so a tail's kernel never
  stalls, and one that does is reported rather than waited out.
- `wait_out_clock_refusal(sim: &Sim, boot: impl FnMut() -> Result<Option<T>, String>) -> Result<Option<T>, String>`
  — that wait, as a loop. It calls `boot` (your boot and kernel, returning
  `Ok(Some(_))` once booted, `Ok(None)` when it gave the run up, and the error's
  text otherwise) and returns what it returns, unless the error is a clock stop
  or refusal that `clock_fallout` excuses and that names an instant. Then it
  sleeps one second past that instant, restarts the process, and calls `boot`
  again, twice at most: a third refusal is an `Err` that fails the run, `the
  boot was refused for the clock a third time, … a platform clock defect, not
  the app's: report it with this run's seed. The third refusal: <refusal>`,
  and never a give-up. Any other error, the stall stop included, comes back
  unchanged. Call it after `sim.quiesce_clock_faults()`; `Drive::recover`
  runs it around the tail's boot, so only a workload below the helper calls
  it.
- `replays_identically(seed: u64, workload: impl Fn(&mut Sim) -> Result<T, String>) -> Result<(), String>`
